RetroClips

Ten seconds of film history. Twenty seconds of why it matters.

Do you love classic movies? So do we — we built this hoping you'll fall for one you've never seen, one shot at a time. A lot of early film history is underseen, under-preserved, or just plain forgotten, and we don't think it should be — this is our small effort to help keep it in circulation.

Shot in about six days for roughly $20,000 by a Poverty Row studio, Detour turns its own cheapness into style -- fog, shadow, and a murder the hero insists was just bad luck. Al narrates the whole film as a man fate keeps tripping, and this scene is the moment the audience has to decide whether to believe him. It's since been restored by the Academy Film Archive and inducted into the National Film Registry. Pabst cast an American unknown, Louise Brooks, over every established German star being considered, and her performance as Lulu -- pure appetite, no shame about it, destroyed by a world that punishes women for exactly that -- is still the reason the film is discussed today. Widely credited as the first commercially successful feature-length documentary, though 'documentary' undersells how staged it was: the man billed as Nanook was really Allakariallak, some of the hunting techniques shown had already been abandoned in favor of rifles, and Flaherty had his cast re-enact a version of traditional life for the camera. It's still one of the founding arguments in an argument documentary filmmaking has never fully settled -- how much reconstruction a 'true' record can contain. A 16-minute collaboration between Luis Buñuel and Salvador Dalí, built from dream logic rather than plot -- ants crawling from a hand, a severed hand in the street, a man dragging two grand pianos loaded with dead donkeys. None of it outlasted the opening image: a straight razor drawn across an open eye, cut together with a cloud slicing the moon so the audience's mind does the cutting for it. (The eye belonged to a calf, not the actress -- a substitution convincing enough that it's still routinely mistaken for real.) It became the founding text of surrealist cinema and one of the most analyzed sixteen minutes in film history. Dwain Esper built a career selling lurid B-pictures as public-health warnings, padding each one with fake “educational” title cards on mental illness to dodge obscenity laws while delivering exactly the shock content the cards claimed to warn against. Maniac -- a barely-coherent riff on Poe's “The Black Cat” and “Murders in the Rue Morgue” -- is the most notorious example: a deranged Maxwell, hiding inside the identity of the mad scientist he murdered, catches a cat and eats its eye. Film historians generally agree the eye was a rigged prop rather than a real animal's, but the scene became exploitation cinema's most cited party trick regardless. By the early 1930s, more than half of US states had eugenics laws on the books, and tens of thousands of Americans -- prisoners, psychiatric patients, the poor -- had been forcibly sterilized under them, a practice the Supreme Court upheld in Buck v. Bell (“three generations of imbeciles are enough,” Oliver Wendell Holmes wrote for the majority). Tomorrow's Children turned that policy into a ticking-clock melodrama: a seventeen-year-old ordered sterilized because of her parents' problems, and a race to stop the surgeons before it's too late. The filmmaking is clumsy, but the target was real, and versions of the law it argues against stayed on the books in some states into the 1970s. D.O.A. opens with its whole premise front-loaded: Frank Bigelow, poisoned with a slow-acting toxin he can't survive, spends the rest of the film investigating who killed him and why, racing a clock that's already run out. Edmond O'Brien plays the reveal completely straight, delivering "I want to report a murder... mine" without a wink, and the gambit worked well enough that the fatally-poisoned-man setup has been recycled by a stage musical, a 1969 West German remake, a 1988 Dennis Quaid version, and a 2022 reboot -- none of which needed permission, since the original fell into the public domain decades ago. Beat the Devil was written day-by-day during shooting -- John Huston and a 29-year-old Truman Capote reworking pages each morning for that day's scenes, with Humphrey Bogart (who co-produced and financed it) reportedly baffled by what the finished film was even supposed to be. Contemporary audiences mostly agreed, and it flopped; decades later it's better understood as an early spoof of the prestige-thriller genre Bogart himself helped define, deadpan enough that people still argue about which lines are meant to be jokes. Roger Corman shot the entire film in two days and a night on sets left over from another production, mostly to test how fast a feature could be made on a bet. He never bothered securing the copyright, evidently not expecting it to have value beyond a quick theatrical run -- which is exactly why it's free to use today, while the 1986 musical remake it inspired stayed firmly copyrighted. This dental-office scene is also where a 23-year-old Jack Nicholson turns up in one of his first film roles, as the patient who shows up next and can't wait for his turn in the chair. The falling building front weighed about two tons, and the attic window was sized to clear Keaton's body by only a few inches on either side -- the crew reportedly couldn't bear to watch, and Keaton insisted on doing the stunt himself, marking his exact spot on the ground beforehand. There was no trick photography: one camera, one take, and a genuinely lethal margin for error if the wind had pushed the facade even slightly off its rig. It's routinely cited as the single most dangerous shot of the silent era, and stunt coordinators still study it today. Getting Keaton to appear seamlessly inside a rapid series of environments -- a desert, a busy street, a mountain ledge, the open ocean -- required none of the compositing tools that would later make this kind of effect routine; in 1924 it meant surveying each location in advance, chalking Keaton's exact mark, and matching the camera's height, distance, and lens precisely between setups so the cut from one world to the next would land as a jolt instead of an obvious scene change. It's still cited as one of the most technically demanding effects sequences of the silent era, achieved with nothing but a tape measure and exact repetition. Universal built a full-scale reproduction of the Notre Dame plaza on its studio lot -- reportedly the most expensive set built in Hollywood up to that point -- and populated it with thousands of extras for the film's climactic siege. Lon Chaney designed and built his own Quasimodo makeup and body rig, including a twenty-to-thirty-pound rubber hump and harness he wore through the entire shoot in the California sun. The "sanctuary" the film's plot hinges on was real medieval law: a church genuinely could shelter a fugitive from secular arrest, at least temporarily, and that specific legal technicality is what the climax turns on. Willis O'Brien's stop-motion effects here were the first time mass audiences had seen dinosaurs move and interact with a live-action world at this scale, and the techniques he refined -- posable armature models, incremental frame-by-frame animation, miniatures matted into real footage -- became the direct blueprint for his own King Kong eight years later. Three years before the film even opened, Arthur Conan Doyle previewed O'Brien's test reel -- a Triceratops family, an Allosaurus attack, a Stegosaurus -- for a room of magicians that included Harry Houdini, coyly calling the creatures "psychic" and letting the room debate whether they'd just watched something real. In 1998 the Library of Congress added the finished film to the National Film Registry. Every figure on screen is a hand-cut, hinged cardboard-and-lead-foil silhouette, animated a fraction of a millimeter at a time and shot frame by frame in a friend's garage by a crew of five. To fake real depth, Reiniger stacked her silhouettes across horizontal panes of glass at different distances from the camera and moved them independently -- a multiplane setup she worked out roughly a decade before Walt Disney's studio patented and popularized its own version. The film took about five years to complete. Because the two earlier animated features by Quirino Cristiani in Argentina no longer survive, Prince Achmed stands as the oldest surviving animated feature film. The village beneath Mephisto's wings is a miniature model, not a full-size set -- art director Robert Herlth's team built it from reeds and rushes standing in for pine trees, glass wool for clouds, and real turf glued onto plaster, with the buildings' proportions deliberately warped to read as vast, crooked distance under the demon's shadow. Emil Jannings plays Mephisto here, a few years before he'd move to Hollywood and become the first person to win the Academy Award for Best Actor, for two other films. Murnau himself considered the picture troubled -- he reshot the ending after a poor test screening -- but this looming apparition over the model village became one of the most reproduced single images of the silent era. The bazaar set alone covered more than two acres on a concrete floor that had to be re-enameled several times a week, part of a production budget over $1.1 million -- an enormous sum for 1924 -- under design chief William Cameron Menzies, whose soaring, geometric sets here launched his career and helped invent what the industry would later call production design. Filming ran more than 28 weeks. Douglas Fairbanks, who produced and starred, did his own stunts and insisted on practical in-camera effects for the flying carpet and the rest of the film's magic rather than the optical trickery available at the time. Adapted from Johnston McCulley's pulp serial "The Curse of Capistrano," this was Fairbanks's first costume swashbuckler after a decade of contemporary comedies, and its success reoriented the rest of his career toward the swordfights and derring-do he's remembered for. Fairbanks did the bulk of his own stunt work and fencing here, athletic enough that decades later Bob Kane cited this exact film -- the mask, the cape, the double identity of a foppish nobleman hiding a masked vigilante -- as a direct model for Batman. This was Paul Robeson's first film role, and he plays two parts -- the corrupt "Reverend" seen here, and that man's honest twin brother -- a dual performance Micheaux built the entire film around. Micheaux wrote, directed, produced, and distributed the picture independently outside the studio system, one of the so-called "race films" made explicitly for Black audiences at a time when most American theaters were segregated. New York's censors found its portrait of a fraudulent preacher offensive enough that they forced Micheaux to cut the original nine-reel version down to five before it could screen at all; that shortened cut is the only version known to survive. The stunt was faked, brilliantly: the sail was pre-slit, Fairbanks gripped a fixed blade rigged to a hidden pulley-and-counterbalance system his own brother Robert engineered, and his weight on the rig lowered him smoothly to the deck while the canvas tore open around him -- airplane propellers off camera billowed the sails for effect. It's also one of the very first color feature films: shot entirely in an early two-strip Technicolor process, only the third feature ever to use it, requiring two strips of film fused back-to-back, so thick and heat-sensitive the picture would warp out of focus during projection. Fairbanks, in his forties by then, still did the stunt work himself, taping his arms and legs to avoid rope burns. Alla Nazimova produced this herself and, though her husband Charles Bryant received the director's credit, most who worked on it -- and most historians since -- consider Nazimova its real director. A persistent rumor holds she cast the entire production with gay and bisexual performers as a tribute to Oscar Wilde; one extra later said gay cast members were indeed present, just not an unusual number of them, let alone all. Costume and set designer Natacha Rambova built every frame directly from Aubrey Beardsley's scandalous 1890s illustrations for Wilde's play -- the film's own opening credits bill her work as "after Aubrey Beardsley." It flopped on release and effectively ended Nazimova's career as a major studio star; it's since been reclaimed as a cult classic. Made for about $5,700 and grossing roughly $450,000, this was the film that established Universal as a major studio. Its plot turns on an early piece of surveillance fiction: the missing girl's father, a deaf inventor, has built a phonographic recording device, and his daughter uses it to secretly capture the trafficking ring's own voices as evidence against them. Marketed as an exposé of the real "white slavery" panic gripping American cities at the time, it was a sensation on release, drawing both audiences and moral reformers -- one of the earliest American feature films built explicitly as a message picture. The Library of Congress added it to the National Film Registry in 2006. Made for about $5,700 and grossing roughly $450,000, this was the film that established Universal as a major studio. Griffith built this Babylon set to a scale nothing in film had attempted before -- walls and towering statuary reportedly visible for miles across Hollywood, populated with some 3,000 extras for its crowd scenes, standing for years afterward as a local landmark before it was finally torn down. He made the film partly as his answer to the firestorm of criticism over his previous picture, The Birth of a Nation: an epic about the destructive cost of intolerance across four different eras of history, crosscut together in a way virtually no one had tried at feature length before. It was a costly commercial failure on release and contributed to Griffith's later financial troubles, but its editing techniques went on to influence nearly every filmmaker who saw it. Lillian Gish did her own stunts here, no double, on real breaking ice during a New England blizzard in temperatures below zero -- about twenty takes a day for three weeks left her with frostbitten fingers and nerve damage in the hand she trailed in the freezing water, feeling she said she never fully got back. Griffith himself was frostbitten on one side of his face directing the scene. Gish had spent the weeks beforehand taking daily ice baths and walking the streets coatless to prepare her body for the cold. None of it was faked: the ice really was breaking apart under them as the cameras rolled. Theda Bara plays "The Vampire" -- never given an actual name -- and the film made her one of the first manufactured movie stars, complete with a fabricated backstory claiming she was born in the shadow of the Sphinx to a French artist and an Arabian princess (she was actually from Cincinnati). Its intertitle "Kiss me, my fool!" became one of the most quoted lines of the silent era, endlessly repeated and misquoted as "kiss me, you fool" for decades after. The film adapts a 1909 Broadway play, itself inspired by Rudyard Kipling's poem "The Vampire," and it's largely responsible for popularizing the word "vamp" as shorthand for a seductive femme fatale. Paul Wegener not only co-directed but plays the Golem himself, under makeup and a heavy clay-textured suit designed by Expressionist architect Hans Poelzig. The film is a prequel to two earlier Golem films Wegener had already made and lost, and it's the one that survives complete. Its blocky, jagged medieval-ghetto sets and the Golem's own lumbering, silent menace fed directly into Hollywood horror a decade later -- Boris Karloff's Frankenstein's Monster owes a visible debt to Wegener's performance and silhouette. Cooper and Schoedsack shot this with no actors, no script, and barely any budget, following the Bakhtiari people of Persia on their real, brutal migration over the Zagros Mountains in search of grazing land -- fording an icy river and then climbing an near-vertical, snowbound pass, on foot, with their herds. The two filmmakers were so taken with adventure filmmaking after this that they went on to make King Kong together eight years later. Grass is now preserved in the National Film Registry as one of the earliest feature-length documentaries. Hitchcock always called this his first true film -- the first to show "the Hitchcock touch." He was 27, working from a novel loosely inspired by Jack the Ripper, and already reaching for the visual tricks that would define his career: a glass floor built into the set so the camera could look straight up through the ceiling at the lodger's pacing feet, and a wrongly-suspected man at the center of the plot, a theme Hitchcock would return to again and again over the next five decades. Star Ivor Novello was already a matinee idol, which forced the studio to soften the ending so its heartthrob couldn't turn out to be the killer. McCay, already famous for the comic strip Little Nemo, hand-drew every one of Gertie's roughly 10,000 frames himself and originally performed the film live on vaudeville stages, standing beside the screen with a whip, "commanding" Gertie to bow, dance, and cry on cue as if she were really responding to him. She was the first animated character ever given a distinct, appealing personality rather than just a gag-delivery device, which makes Gertie the direct ancestor of every cartoon character with a face audiences actually cared about, from Mickey Mouse onward. This was John Ford's first big-budget epic, made when he was still in his twenties, and Fox threw real resources at it: thousands of extras, cavalry, Chinese and Irish laborers, herds of buffalo, and two replica locomotives built to match the original Jupiter and No. 119 engines down to the rivets. Ford shot much of it on location in the Nevada desert in brutal winter conditions, and the finished film helped define the Western epic as a genre a full generation before Ford's own Stagecoach. Wings won the first-ever Academy Award for Best Picture and remains the only fully silent film to do so. Director William Wellman, a World War I combat pilot himself, insisted on shooting real aerial combat with cameras mounted directly on the planes rather than using models, which meant training his stars, including Clara Bow and a young, then-unknown Gary Cooper in a small early role, to fly. The production borrowed actual Army Air Corps pilots and aircraft, and several stunt fliers were injured during filming chasing shots no one had attempted before. The Covered Wagon was the picture that proved the Western could be an event, not just a two-reel programmer. Paramount sent director James Cruze and a full production unit deep into Utah and Nevada to shoot with real wagon trains, real livestock, and hundreds of extras fording an actual river rather than a studio tank, and audiences in 1923 had never seen anything like it. It became one of the biggest box-office hits of the silent era and set the template every big-budget Western since, from Wagon Master to Red River, has followed. The Big Parade was the film that made King Vidor a top-tier director and John Gilbert a superstar, and it stayed MGM's highest-grossing silent picture for years. Vidor shot the farewell sequence, a French village girl clinging to a departing supply truck as her soldier sweetheart is hauled away to the front, almost entirely with actors and extras rather than trick photography, and it became one of the most reproduced images of the silent era. The film's unsentimental battle scenes, filmed with Army cooperation and real veterans as extras, were as influential on later war pictures as its romance was on every farewell scene that followed. This is the first-ever film adaptation of Frankenstein, made by Thomas Edison's own studio just twelve years after cinema itself was born. Director J. Searle Dawley created the monster's creation scene by burning a papier-mache dummy in a controlled fire and filming it, then running that footage in reverse, so the creature appears to assemble itself out of smoke and flame rather than fall apart. It's one of the earliest documented in-camera special effects in film history, and the only surviving print for decades was a private collector's copy, not rediscovered by the public until the 1970s. He Who Gets Slapped was the very first film released by the newly formed Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer, and it made Lon Chaney one of the studio's defining stars before he ever put on the makeup he's best remembered for. Chaney plays a humiliated scientist who reinvents himself as a circus clown whose entire act is being slapped in the face by his fellow performers while the audience howls, a running bit that Chaney plays as pure showmanship on the surface and quiet devastation underneath. The image of the laughing-on-the-outside tragic clown, endlessly reproduced since, traces directly back to this performance. Seven Chances closes with one of the most celebrated physical sequences in silent comedy: Buster Keaton, fleeing an ever-growing mob, stumbles into a real avalanche of boulders and has to outrun them down an actual hillside. Keaton did the stunt himself with no safety rigging, dodging a mix of real rocks and oversized papier-mache boulders built to roll convincingly at speed, and the sequence was reportedly added only after a test screening got a bigger laugh from an accidental rockslide than anything else in the film. It's been cited by directors from Jackie Chan to Edgar Wright as a benchmark for what practical stunt comedy can do. Man with a Movie Camera is a city-symphony documentary with no actors, no sets, and no intertitles, built entirely from a single day in Soviet urban life and Dziga Vertov's belief that the camera could see truth the human eye couldn't. This opening image, a cameraman dwarfed atop his own giant apparatus, announces the film's constant self-awareness: it shows its own editor at work, its own audience watching it, and its own camera being carried into traffic and up factory scaffolding to get the shot. It topped Sight & Sound's directors' and critics' polls decades later as one of the greatest documentaries ever made. Cabiria was the era's defining spectacle picture, an internationally distributed sensation that directly shaped D.W. Griffith's Intolerance and set the template for every 'cast of thousands' epic that followed. Director Giovanni Pastrone staged Hannibal's crossing of the Alps with real elephants and hundreds of extras on an actual mountainside rather than a studio backlot, and the film's title cards were reportedly the first to credit a poet, Gabriele D'Annunzio, giving the production literary prestige it used to market itself worldwide. It also introduced Maciste, one of cinema's first recurring action heroes, who went on to star in dozens of his own films. Aelita: Queen of Mars was Soviet cinema's first venture into science fiction, built around a Martian civilization designed by Constructivist artist Alexandra Exter, whose jutting geometric sets and armor-plated costumes drew directly on Cubist and Suprematist theory rather than anything from earlier fantasy filmmaking. The angular, alien production design is frequently cited as a direct visual precursor to Metropolis, released three years later. Its box-office success made the queen played by Yuliya Solntseva, an enduring image of Soviet-era science fiction, reproduced on posters and book covers for decades after. Gulliver's Travels was Fleischer Studios' answer to Disney's Snow White, and only the second animated feature ever released, rushed into production specifically to prove Max and Dave Fleischer could compete at feature length. The waking-on-the-beach sequence, Gulliver dwarfing an entire kingdom's worth of tiny staked-down ropes, became the single most reproduced image from the film and the one most audiences still remember. Its copyright was never renewed at the required interval, a lapse that also freed Popeye and Superman's earliest Fleischer cartoons decades later, though this is the studio's only full animated feature to fall into the public domain this way. The Passion of Joan of Arc is built almost entirely out of faces in extreme close-up, an approach so radical for 1928 that Carl Dreyer had sets built and then largely refused to show them, trusting Renee Jeanne Falconetti's performance to carry the film alone. She reportedly never acted again after this role, and film historians still debate how much of her visible anguish was performance versus Dreyer's famously punishing directing methods. The film was thought lost for decades until a nearly pristine print turned up in a Norwegian mental institution's closet in 1981. A Page of Madness has no intertitles at all, telling its story entirely through Teinosuke Kinugasa's rapid-fire editing, double exposures, and expressionist staging, a technique closer to European avant-garde cinema than anything else being made in Japan at the time. The film was believed lost for over 40 years until Kinugasa found a surviving print in his own storehouse in 1971. It remains one of the only widely available windows into 1920s Japanese avant-garde film, a movement almost entirely wiped out by the reels lost in the following decades. Carnival of Souls was made on a shoestring budget by an industrial-film director, Herk Harvey, who financed it himself and shot it in three weeks using a cast of mostly local actors. It flopped on release and was barely seen again until it turned up on late-night television in the 1970s, where its dreamlike dread found the cult audience the theatrical run never did. Directors from George Romero to David Lynch have cited it as a direct influence, and the film's copyright lapsed into the public domain almost immediately after release when the required renewal was never filed. The Immigrant is one of Chaplin's most acclaimed Mutual shorts, added to the National Film Registry in 1998 for its blend of physical comedy and genuine sympathy for the immigrant experience it depicts. The ship-set opening was filmed on a set mechanically rigged to rock back and forth, sending Chaplin, his fellow actors, and their soup sliding in unison, a practical effect that took real engineering to pull off in 1917. It remains one of the clearest early showcases of Chaplin's gift for turning physical discomfort into pure comic rhythm. Speedy was Harold Lloyd's last silent film, shot largely on real New York City streets rather than a studio backlot, giving it an almost documentary quality of 1920s Manhattan that few other films of the era captured. Babe Ruth appears as himself in a genuine cameo, playing along with the joke that his own reckless cab ride to Yankee Stadium is nearly as thrilling as anything he does on the field. The location shoot reportedly drew real crowds who had no idea they were watching a movie being made, some of whom ended up in the finished film. Blackmail was Britain's first sound feature, and Alfred Hitchcock famously shot it as a silent film and then, mid-production, reshot key scenes with dialogue once talkies became unavoidable, making it a genuine hybrid of two eras of cinema. The climactic chase across the British Museum's Reading Room dome combined real location footage with matte paintings and miniature work, an early example of the composite trickery Hitchcock would keep refining for the rest of his career. It's routinely cited as the moment his visual signature, vertiginous heights, silhouettes, landmark set pieces, first fully arrived. Feline Follies is the film where Felix the Cat effectively began, released under the name Master Tom a year before the character was rebranded and became one of the first cartoon characters to achieve real global fame, predating Mickey Mouse by nearly a decade. Animator Otto Messmer worked under producer Pat Sullivan's name, a common arrangement in the era's animation studios, and it would be decades before Messmer's authorship of Felix was widely credited. The character's rubbery, expressive movement style set the template for cartoon animals that Disney and others would build on through the rest of the silent era. Ladislas Starevich made this entirely with dead insects rigged into articulated stop-motion puppets, reportedly a workaround after his live beetles refused to perform under studio lights. The technique was so far ahead of anything else being attempted with animation that some contemporary audiences assumed the insects had been trained rather than animated frame by frame, and Starevich never fully explained his methods. It stands as one of the earliest and strangest examples of stop-motion character animation, made in Moscow a full generation before King Kong or the Rankin-Bass holiday specials it quietly anticipates. Segundo de Chomon is often called the Spanish Melies, and The Electric Hotel is his best-known surviving trick film, built almost entirely from stop-motion effects where luggage packs itself, boots lace themselves, and hair styles itself with no operator ever entering the frame. Working independently of Melies's own studio, Chomon achieved some of the era's most convincing object animation through frame-by-frame pixilation, painstakingly repositioning each item a fraction at a time between exposures. The film's premise, an imaginary hotel where every mundane task happens automatically, reads almost like an accidental prediction of a century of home-automation advertising. Master of the House is Dreyer at his most disciplined: nearly the entire film unfolds inside one cramped Copenhagen apartment, and he insisted on building it as a real, fully wired flat rather than a set, so his actors could move through it the way people actually move through a home they have lived in for years. The film's real subject is housework itself, filmed with the same patient attention Dreyer would later bring to Falconetti's face in The Passion of Joan of Arc, and it was a massive hit in Denmark precisely because audiences recognized the unglamorous domestic labor nobody else was bothering to point a camera at. This is the silent, biblical-prologue half of DeMille's first Ten Commandments, made three decades before his own more famous 1956 remake with Charlton Heston, and the Red Sea effect here was achieved by combining footage of real waves with a giant tank and traveling matte work that was considered borderline miraculous in 1923. DeMille buried an entire full-scale Egyptian city set, sphinxes and all, in the Guadalupe-Nipomo Dunes in California after filming wrapped rather than pay to haul it out, and archaeologists have spent decades since digging pieces of it back up. Applause was one of the first sound films to break out of the static, camera-locked-in-a-booth phase early talkies were stuck in, since Mamoulian insisted on a moving camera and even rigged two separate soundtracks so dialogue and singing could overlap, something the studio's engineers told him was technically impossible. He came to Hollywood straight from directing Broadway, and it shows in how the film treats the stage number itself as the point rather than as a scene to cut away from, holding wide on the full house the way a live audience actually would have seen it.
